K8s · Booking Platform
01 / 0705:00
Five-minute architecture walkthrough

From one Node.js app to a resilient platform.

I built a Booking-style Kubernetes lab to understand who runs applications, who routes traffic, what happens during failure, and how production releases stay safe.

Runtime
Pods

One running instance of a microservice, containing its application container.

Control
Deployments

Maintain replica count, replace failed Pods, and roll out new versions.

Network
Services

Provide stable discovery and balance traffic across Ready Pods.

Opening — 35 sec: “I wanted to learn Kubernetes through a realistic system, not a hello-world container. So I modeled booking, hotels, payments and an API gateway.”
01
Request path

Three layers of traffic control.

Global traffic manager
chooses region
→
Ingress / Cloud LB
enters cluster
→
Kubernetes Service
chooses Ready Pod
→
Application Pod
handles request
Gateway responsibility

Edge policy

Authentication, coarse rate limiting, routing, request aggregation and correlation IDs.

Microservice responsibility

Business correctness

Authorization, domain limits, validation, structured logs, metrics and traces.

Request flow — 40 sec: “Pods never balance traffic themselves. A Kubernetes Service balances inside one cluster; Ingress accepts external traffic; a global layer selects a healthy region.”
02
Production view

Regions, clusters, namespaces and data.

Each region has an independent cluster. Inside the namespace, Services route to replicated Gateway, Booking, Hotels and Payment Pods. PostgreSQL spans availability zones and replicates to a disaster-recovery region.

Multi-region routing
Multi-AZ placement
Primary + replicas
Backups and restore drills
Architecture — 50 sec: Zoom the browser if needed. Explain Region → Cluster → Namespace. Point out that the database operator, not a normal Service, performs primary election.
03
Interactive failure

A Pod dies mid-request. What now?

Booking
Pod A
Booking
Pod B
Booking
Pod C
All three Pods are Ready. The Service can route to any of them.
Current request

May fail

An in-flight connection cannot magically move to another Pod.

Recovery

Desired state wins

Deployment creates a replacement; Service sends new traffic only to Ready Pods.

Safety

Retry carefully

Timeouts, idempotency keys, transactions and circuit breakers prevent duplicate writes.

Failure — 45 sec: Click “Simulate Pod failure.” Stress that payment retries must use an idempotency key; a blind retry can charge twice.
04
State and secrets

Stateless Pods. Durable data.

Primary
read/write
Replica 1
read-only
Replica 2
read-only
Operator monitors health; replicas stream changes from Primary.
Configuration

ConfigMap

Non-sensitive URLs, log level and static configuration. Connected only to explicitly selected workloads.

Credentials

Secret Manager / Vault

Short-lived credentials delivered to authorized service accounts. Never commit real keys to Git.

Data — 45 sec: Click “Fail primary.” Explain quorum, promotion and stable DB endpoint. Kubernetes Service does not elect the primary; the database operator does.
05
Safe feature delivery

A feature targets traffic—not random Pods.

Canary rollout

Stable v1 90% · Canary v2 10%

Metrics decide whether v2 is promoted or rolled back.

Feature flag

Same code, selected audience

Enable by user, cohort, region or percentage without choosing individual Pods and without a new deployment.

Error rate
p95 / p99 latency
Business KPI
SLO budget
Releases — 45 sec: Differentiate feature flags from canary deployments. Rolling updates create temporary surge; blue/green temporarily runs two complete fleets.
06
What production adds

Kubernetes runs workloads.
Reliability is a system design.

Observe

Logs · Metrics · Traces

Centralized telemetry, dashboards, SLOs and actionable alerts.

Scale

HPA + capacity tests

Replica count follows traffic, latency targets, Pod capacity and failure headroom.

Protect

Defense in depth

WAF, rate limits, RBAC, network policy, secret rotation and image scanning.

Next: add PostgreSQL, Ingress, Helm, autoscaling, observability and CI/CD to the local Booking lab.

Close — 30 sec: “The biggest lesson is separation of responsibility. Deployments control lifecycle, Services route traffic, applications protect business correctness, and data systems protect state.”
07
